Model syllabus

Great works on mind, across languages and cultures.

A proposed ten-week course shaped by the WATER course’s sustained encounters with shared works, community events and writing. Multicultural inquiry organizes the slate from beginning to end.

The proposed slateWords for mindTerm sequence

The course

A dream can undo certainty. A practiced movement can exceed a verbal explanation. Another person’s judgment can enter our experience of ourselves. The works in this course examine mind through philosophical argument, religious cultivation, poetry, music and the telling of a life.

We begin with words and works that do not divide thought, feeling, body and self in the same ways. Each work has its own language, history and purposes. Contemporary neuroscience and AI research enter this conversation as further accounts to examine. No single tradition supplies the definition that all the others must fit.

Students need no previous philosophy or neuroscience. We begin with a scene, passage, sound or image; follow the work’s argument and form; then develop interpretations that can withstand close reading and disagreement.

What is a mind?

Why do we mind?

How do minds, sports, and art all interact?

What does it mean if we don’t know mind?

Six sustained works: a proposed slate

These selections deal directly with mental life: its cultivation, its certainty, its relation to the body, and its formation among other people. They are candidates for faculty discussion, not an approved reading list. Each receives time for close reading; the course returns to earlier works as the comparisons develop.

Weeks 1–2Early Chinese philosophical literature

Zhuangzi · The Inner Chapters

A butterfly dream, Cook Ding’s practiced movement, and the fasting of the heart-mind.

Intellectual reach. Perspective, transformation and the limits of fixed judgments. The stories make difficult philosophy available through concrete scenes.

Proposed reading & source

The seven Inner Chapters. Robert Eno’s university-hosted translation supplies an accessible starting edition; compare translation choices before adoption.

Zhuangzi: The Inner Chapters

Week 3Early Buddhist verse in Pāli

Dhammapada · Sayings of the Dhamma

Brief verses describe an unsettled mind and the work of cultivating it.

Intellectual reach. Attention, desire, conduct and liberation. Read mental training within the work’s Buddhist purposes.

Proposed reading & source

The complete short verse collection, with close reading of the opening and Cittavagga, verses 33–43. Proposed translation: Bhikkhu Sujato.

Dhammapada / Sayings of the Dhamma

Week 4Islamic philosophical and spiritual autobiography

Al-Ghazālī · Deliverance from Error

A scholar’s confidence in what he knows gives way to searching doubt.

Intellectual reach. Perception, reason, certainty and Sufi practice. A Persian author writing in Arabic develops an account that deserves study on its own terms.

Proposed reading & source

The complete short work. Select a modern scholarly translation; the linked historical version enables an initial comparison.

Deliverance from Error / al-Munqidh min al-ḍalāl

Week 5Early modern European philosophy, written in Latin

René Descartes · Meditations on First Philosophy

Dreaming and doubt unsettle ordinary certainty; the thinker examines what remains.

Intellectual reach. The thinking self, knowledge and embodiment. Compare the argument with al-Ghazālī without assuming either agreement or direct influence.

Proposed reading & source

Meditations I, II and VI, with a short guide to III–V. The complete six meditations remain available for deeper reading.

Meditations on First Philosophy

Weeks 6–7African American essays, history and music

W. E. B. Du Bois · The Souls of Black Folk

A person encounters the self through other people’s racialized judgments.

Intellectual reach. Double-consciousness, social recognition and the relation between inward life and public power. The Sorrow Songs make listening central.

Proposed reading & source

Forethought and chapters I, III, XI, XIII and XIV. Retain the musical epigraphs and pair chapter XIV with historically contextualized recordings selected with music faculty.

The Souls of Black Folk

Weeks 8–10Modern Japanese novel

Natsume Sōseki · Kokoro

A young man tries to understand the private life of a person he calls Sensei.

Intellectual reach. Heart, mind, secrecy and responsibility. Narrative makes knowing another person a different undertaking from explaining a mechanism.

Proposed reading & source

The complete novel over three weeks. Confirm the translation and divide readings by that edition. Its extended narrative gives the course time to develop and revise interpretations.

Kokoro

Six works cannot represent the world. This candidate slate still needs stronger representation of women’s sustained accounts, African traditions beyond the African American selection, Indigenous thought and Korean sources. New candidates should change the intellectual conversation and receive real teaching time. The existing bank retains other possible selections.

The word “mind” has a history

English mind comes through Old English gemynd, associated with memory and thought. Its linguistic ancestry connects it with Latin mens and Sanskrit manas. This traces an English word; it does not identify the moment humans discovered mental life. Word-history source.

Everyday English already gives us several uses: “keep in mind,” “change your mind,” “mind the step,” and “I don’t mind.” Remembering, deciding, attending and objecting are related uses, not identical activities.

Words for mind across languages

This is a small, sourced comparison, not a list of interchangeable translations. Ancient textual usages and modern dictionary senses are labeled separately. The original word stays beside its translation throughout the course.

Hear words for mind · Human voices

mind / gemynd

English · historical

Memory and thought in the word’s Old English history. Present English includes remembering, attending and objecting. Source

noos / nous

Ancient Greek

Perception, thought and understanding. Distinguish this from psychē, the soul in Plato’s chariot passage. Source

mens

Latin

Mind, understanding and judgment; one relevant term among several, not a universal technical equivalent. Source

manas

Sanskrit

A term whose range includes thought, intention and feeling. Its technical sense changes with the philosophical school. Source

citta

Pāli · Buddhist text

The term in the Dhammapada’s Cittavagga. Read its cultivation within the verses’ ethical and religious setting. Source

心 · xīn

Chinese · historical

Heart and thinking are connected in the lexical record. “Heart-mind” keeps that overlap visible. Source

qalb / qulūb

Arabic · a textual example

Heart / hearts. Qur’an 22:46 connects hearts with reasoning; this example is not a complete Arabic vocabulary of mind. Source

마음 · maeum

Korean · modern usage

Mind, heart, feeling and intention appear across the dictionary’s senses. This is modern usage, not a claim about ancient etymology. Source

心 / こころ · kokoro

Japanese · modern usage

Mind, heart and spirit are contextual English glosses. A shared character with Chinese does not make usages identical. Source

Shared roots do not guarantee shared meanings. A word’s range does not prove that all its speakers think alike. Translation becomes part of close reading: the passage, period and author determine the relevant sense.

Ancient approaches to mental life

Heart, personhood and judgment

The Greenfield Papyrus offers an Egyptian starting object: the heart has a place in accounts of mind, memory and a person’s continuing existence. Plato’s chariot in Phaedrus 246a–b presents conflict within the soul through an image of driver and horses.

Perspective, practice and liberation

The Zhuangzi and Dhammapada receive sustained study in the slate. Their treatment of mental life connects to ways of acting and living. Their disagreements matter as much as their points of contact.

These are different ancient sources, not stages on a single road toward modern neuroscience. Al-Ghazālī, Descartes, Du Bois and Sōseki belong to later historical settings; the course keeps that chronology visible.

Poetry, music, art and sport throughout the term

Short shared encounters recur alongside the six longer works. They give the class other forms of evidence and expression without adding a new major reading every week.

Poetry and listening

Read Dickinson’s The Brain—is wider than the Sky and I felt a Funeral, in my Brain in full. Return to rhythm, syntax and the difference between a speaker and an author. With Du Bois, keep the Sorrow Songs and musical epigraphs integral to the reading.

Action and shared attention

Study Lygia Clark’s Brazilian participatory work Caminhando through its documentation. Listen to Steve Reich’s Music for 18 Musicians. Bring an athlete’s and a musician’s accounts of trained action into conversation with Cook Ding.

Proposed common events: a translation session; a musician–artist–athlete session on practice; and a conversation about current mind research. Speakers, recordings and dates remain to be arranged. Describing a skill, interpreting an artwork and measuring performance remain distinct kinds of work.

Current research in conversation with the works

The learning bank supports two levels of access: a plain-language account and a manageable source passage for the common course; the complete paper, methods and counterarguments for further study. Research companions are introduced where they sharpen a comparison.

Mark Solms

Feeling and consciousness

The Hidden Spring introduction provides an accessible entry to his account. It can accompany the course’s comparisons of heart, mind and body.

Michael Levin

Cognition across scales

The tissue study opens a comparison between organized biological behavior and experience. Complexity alone does not establish feeling.

Cameron Berg

Claims about AI experience

The self-report study brings the problem of interpreting another mind into a new setting. Read it alongside a competing account and the reported AI correspondence.

None of these accounts is the course’s prescribed answer. Their full technical papers remain available in the bank. Sacks and Le Guin also remain there as alternative sustained works for a later slate.

A possible term sequence

Three meetings per week, with community events taking the place of selected class meetings. This is a pacing model; term dates, holidays and exact reading divisions are not yet set.

Week 1–2

Zhuangzi

Begin the language comparison. Read the Inner Chapters and the short Egyptian and Greek companion sources. Return to practiced movement in Cook Ding.

Writing: Opening reflection; Summary at the end of week 2.

Week 3

Dhammapada

Read the verse collection; examine mental cultivation and liberation. A translation event can develop the distinctions among citta, manas and heart-mind.

Writing: Workbook and preparation for synthesis.

Week 4

Al-Ghazālī

Stay with the short autobiography, its doubt and its religious resolution. Bring its account of certainty into conversation with earlier works.

Writing: Develop a synthesis across two works.

Week 5

Descartes

Read the selected meditations with the intervening argument explained. Revisit Dickinson’s poems as another way of writing inward experience.

Writing: Synthesis at the end of week 5.

Week 6–7

Du Bois

Read the selected chapters, epigraphs and Sorrow Songs. Shared music, art and sport encounters make embodied and social experience part of the comparison.

Writing: Revise the synthesis using feedback.

Week 8

Kokoro · begin

Begin the full novel. Keep original-language terms available while developing an interpretation of another person’s inner life.

Writing: Revision of the Synthesis at the end of week 8.

Week 9–10

Kokoro · continue and complete

Complete the novel. A research event connects Solms, Levin and Berg with the course’s accumulated distinctions; the full papers remain extensions.

Writing: Final Synthesis and closing reflection at the end of term.

Writing that develops across the term

This model follows the writing structure in Teacher Ma’s current WATER section. It proposes the same lengths and weights below for discussion; these are not claims about a future program requirement.

Proposed writing and participation model
WorkScopeWeight
SummaryNo more than 500 words10%
Synthesis500–750 words15%
Revision of the Synthesis750 words + 50–100-word revision reflection15%
Final Synthesis1,250 words20%
Class participationPreparation, listening and contributions to shared interpretation25%
Reading & Reflection WorkbookOne handwritten page per meeting; event pages completed during or after the event15%

Opening and closing writing reflections accompany the sequence. The final synthesis develops an argument across works while preserving their differences. There is no proposed examination. Assignment instructions and future institutional policies remain to be developed.

From candidate slate to a teachable course

Before adoption, read the selected editions in full, review translations with colleagues, set a sustainable reading load, confirm lawful access and prepare accessible audio and visual alternatives. The bank identifies how deeply each source has been reviewed. The current slate is researched enough to discuss, not yet a completed course reader.

Students should finish able to interpret a work closely, account for a translation choice, compare historically distinct accounts of mind, distinguish an empirical finding from an interpretation, and revise a supported argument. Personal disclosure is not required.

Revision basis: Teacher Ma’s live Fall 2026 WATER syllabus, checked 10 October 2026, and Lawrence’s published WATER slate. This public proposal does not reproduce private course records or adopt existing section policies for a future class.
